en: Looking up, how worthy of reverence: our teachers' kindness.
In the garden of teaching, too, how many years already!
When I think on it, how very swift, these years and months.
Now, indeed, let us part. Come then, farewell.
The kindness of the days when we were close to one another:
even after we part, oh, do not forget it.
Make your way in the world and raise your name; oh, strive hard.
Now, indeed, let us part. Come then, farewell.
The window of learning we grew used to, morning and evening,
the lamplight of fireflies, the piled-up white snow:
there is no moment I forget them, the passing years and months.
Now, indeed, let us part. Come then, farewell.
rom: Aogeba tōtoshi, waga shi no on.
Oshie no niwa ni mo, haya ikutose.
Tagai ni mutsumishi, higoro no on.
Wakaruru nochi ni mo, yayo wasuruna.
Mi o tate na o age, yayo hagemeyo.
Asa yū narenishi, manabi no mado.
Wasururu ma zo naki, yuku toshitsuki.
notes: The romanization follows the words as they are sung, not the historical kana spelling of the 1884 text: あふげば is aogeba, たふとし tōtoshi, おもへば omoeba, ゆふ yū; わかるゝ and わするゝ are wakaruru and wasururu, and いざゝらば is iza saraba (ゝ repeats the kana before it). The particle を is written o. The phrase stops (。) of the original are kept as a comma after the first half of each line and a full stop at its end.

line 1.1: aogeba, 'when (we) look up (to them)', in reverence; tōtoshi, 'precious, worthy of reverence'. 'waga shi' can be 'my teacher' or 'our teachers'; on is a kindness received, a debt of gratitude.
line 1.2: oshie no niwa, 'the garden of teaching', i.e. the school; ikutose, 'how many years'.
line 1.3: toshi (疾し), 'swift'; toshitsuki, 'years and months', the time that has passed.
line 1.4 (and 2.4, 3.4): wakareme is the classical volitional -mu in its -me form after koso: 'now let us part' (or 'now we shall part'), not 'we have parted'. iza saraba, 'well then, farewell'.
line 2.1: higoro no on, 'the kindness of everyday', of the days spent together; mutsumishi, '(we) were close, were on good terms'.
line 2.2 (and 2.3): yayo, an interjection of calling, 'oh'.
line 2.3: mi o tate na o age, 'set up yourself and raise your name', i.e. make your way in life and become known.
line 3.1: manabi no mado, 'the window of learning', the study or schoolroom; narenishi, 'that (we) grew used to'.
line 3.2: the fireflies' light and the snow are an image of study by the poorest light, from an old Chinese tale of students who read by fireflies and by the glow of snow.
line 3.3: wasururu ma zo naki, 'there is no moment of forgetting'; yuku toshitsuki, 'the years and months that go by'.
